title: Firm-by-Firm Guide
tagline: Who the major quant/HFT firms are, what they're known for, and what their interviews emphasize.

concept.analogy: Applying to quant firms without knowing their differences is like auditioning for orchestras without knowing which want a violinist and which want a drummer. They're all elite, but each has a culture, a house style, and signature audition pieces. Knowing them lets you target your prep and your story to what each actually values — and avoid generic answers that signal you didn't do your homework.
paragraphs: The quant/HFT world is a relatively small set of elite firms, broadly in three (overlapping) camps: market makers / prop trading shops (Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Hudson River Trading, Jump Trading, Optiver, IMC, DRW, SIG, Tower, Five Rings, Akuna), hedge-fund-style quant firms (Citadel, Two Sigma, DE Shaw, Jane Street also trades a lot of strategies), and specialized ultra-low-latency / FPGA shops. Roles span quant trading, quant research, quant development, and low-latency systems/FPGA engineering. This lesson gives a high-level orientation — always verify specifics on each firm's current careers page, since processes evolve.

Why firm knowledge matters for interviews: it lets you target the right skills (a mental-math-and-games-heavy trading process vs a C++/systems-heavy dev process), tailor your 'why this firm' story credibly, and set expectations for the rounds. It also helps you choose where to apply: do you want to trade, research signals, build ultra-low-latency C++, or design FPGA pipelines? Different firms lean toward different strengths and cultures.

A caution on stereotypes: reputations ('firm X loves probability puzzles', 'firm Y is all C++ speed') are useful priors but not guarantees — interviewers and teams vary, processes change year to year, and many firms hire across all four tracks. Use the guide to orient and prepare broadly along your track, not to over-fit to a rumored question bank. The durable skills in this module (probability + mental math, C++, systems, microstructure, architecture) are what every one of these firms ultimately filters for.

Finally, the meta-advice: research each firm you apply to via its careers page, engineering/research blog, and any public talks, then connect your genuine interests and projects to what they do. Recruiters and interviewers can tell the difference between a candidate who understands and wants their specific work and one firing off identical applications. Depth of preparation along your track plus authentic, specific motivation is the winning combination.

callouts.title: Verify, don't rely on rumors
callouts.body: Interview formats and question styles change. Use community reports as priors but confirm the current process on the firm's careers page and recruiter emails, and prepare the underlying skills rather than memorizing a rumored question set.

callouts.title: 'Why this firm' must be specific
callouts.body: Reference something real — a paper/talk, the product (e.g., ETF market making), the tech stack (OCaml at Jane Street, heavy C++/FPGA elsewhere), or the research style. Generic answers read as low effort.

deepDive.intro: A high-level orientation to representative firms and what their interviews tend to emphasize (verify current specifics yourself).

steps.title: Jane Street
steps.detail: Famous for a culture of curiosity, clear thinking, and probability/markets reasoning; uses OCaml heavily and values mental models over rote knowledge. Interviews (across trading, research, SWE) lean on probability, expected value, market-making and estimation games, and clear reasoning out loud; SWE roles also test strong CS fundamentals. Great fit if you love thinking about uncertainty and explaining your reasoning.

steps.title: Citadel & Citadel Securities
steps.detail: Citadel is a large multi-strategy hedge fund; Citadel Securities is a leading market maker. Rigorous, role-specific processes: quant research emphasizes statistics/ML and modeling rigor; quant dev/SWE emphasizes strong DS&A and (for low-latency teams) C++/systems; trading emphasizes probability and markets. Expect high bars and multiple technical rounds plus fit.

steps.title: Hudson River Trading (HRT), Jump, Tower
steps.detail: Highly technical, low-latency trading firms with strong engineering cultures. Quant dev/core roles skew hard into algorithms, C++, and systems/performance (caches, concurrency, networking), often with a systems-design or 'make it fast' round and serious DS&A. Excellent fit for those who love low-latency engineering and computer-science depth.

steps.title: Optiver, IMC, DRW, SIG, Akuna, Five Rings
steps.detail: Prominent market makers (often options/derivatives) with strong trading-and-tech cultures. Trading roles famously include fast mental-math tests (e.g., Optiver's arithmetic), probability, and market-making games; tech roles test DS&A and C++/low-latency. SIG is known for poker/decision-making under uncertainty. Great fit for aspiring traders who enjoy games and fast math, and for low-latency devs.

steps.title: Two Sigma, DE Shaw, and research-heavy shops
steps.detail: Quant hedge funds with deep research cultures spanning statistics, ML, and large-scale data engineering (often somewhat longer horizons than pure HFT). Research roles emphasize statistics/ML, modeling rigor, and avoiding overfitting/lookahead; engineering roles emphasize strong software/data systems. Best fit if you lean toward research, modeling, and data at scale.

notes.title: Internships are the main pipeline
notes.detail: For students, summer internships at these firms are the dominant route to full-time offers and convert at high rates — prioritize landing one, and apply early in the cycle.

notes.title: Compensation and competition
notes.detail: These roles are among the best-paid in tech/finance, which is why the bar is so high and recruiting so competitive. That's all the more reason to target and prepare deliberately.

notes.title: Beyond the famous names
notes.detail: Many excellent smaller prop shops and desks exist; the same skill set applies. Don't fixate only on the biggest names — broaden your applications along your track.

complexity.timeReason: Knowing the landscape is quick; the work is preparing the track skills each firm filters for, which this module supplies.

pitfalls: Over-fitting to rumored question banks instead of mastering the underlying skills.
Generic 'why this firm' answers that ignore the firm's actual product, tech, or research.
Assuming all firms test the same thing — trading vs dev vs research processes differ a lot.
Applying only to the biggest names and missing strong fits at smaller shops.
Relying on outdated community reports without verifying the current process.

interviewQuestions.q: Why do you want to work at this firm specifically? (and how should you approach answering it)
a: The answer must be specific and authentic: reference something concrete about the firm — its product or market (e.g., ETF/options market making), its technology or research style (e.g., OCaml and a culture of clear reasoning at Jane Street, deep low-latency C++/FPGA engineering at an HRT/Jump-style shop, statistics/ML research at a Two Sigma/DE Shaw-style fund), a talk or blog post you found compelling, or the specific track and team — and connect it to your genuine interests and projects.

How to approach it: research the firm via its careers page, engineering/research blog, and public talks; pick one or two things that truly resonate with what you want to do (trade, research, build fast systems, design FPGAs); and tie them to evidence from your background. Avoid generic praise ('you're the best/smartest') — interviewers hear it constantly and it signals low effort. Specificity plus honesty is what lands.
followups: What do you know about how we make money?

interviewQuestions.q: How would you decide which type of quant firm/role to target?
a: Match the work to your strengths and interests. If you love decision-making under uncertainty, fast math, and markets, target trading roles at market makers (Optiver, IMC, Jane Street, SIG, etc.). If you love building ultra-fast software and computer-science depth, target quant dev / low-latency systems roles (HRT, Jump, Citadel Securities, Tower) and lean on C++/systems/architecture. If you love statistics, ML, and modeling with data rigor, target quant research at funds like Two Sigma, DE Shaw, or Citadel. If you love hardware, look at FPGA/low-latency specialist roles.

Then weight your preparation to that track's bar (per the hiring-funnel lesson) and apply broadly within it — including smaller shops, not just the famous names. The underlying skills (probability + mental math, C++, systems, microstructure, architecture) transfer across firms, so building them deeply gives you the most options while you decide.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you research a firm well enough to give a credible 'why this firm' and choose a track?
a: Go past the homepage. Read the firm's careers page and specific job description (which tells you the track and the actual interview emphasis), their engineering and/or research blog (reveals tech stack, problems they care about, and culture — e.g., OCaml and clear-reasoning culture at Jane Street, deep low-latency C++/FPGA at HRT/Jump-style shops, statistics/ML research at Two Sigma/DE Shaw-style funds), and any public talks (CppCon, firm tech talks) or podcasts. Note their product/market (market making in equities/options, multi-strategy, etc.) and how they make money.

Use that to (1) craft a specific, authentic 'why this firm' that references something real — a talk, a product, the tech, the research style — connected to your own interests/projects, not generic praise; and (2) choose/confirm your track by matching the firm's strengths to what you want to do (trade, research, build fast systems, design FPGAs). Treat community reports (Glassdoor/forums) as priors to *verify*, not facts, since processes change. The signal you're sending is that you understand and genuinely want *their* work — which recruiters can easily distinguish from a mass application, and which also helps you target the right preparation.

problems.title: Profile three target firms
problems.statement: Choose three firms you'd realistically apply to for your target track. For each, write: their primary business, the role you'd target, what their interview likely emphasizes, a specific authentic reason you're interested, and which sections of this module you'd review before interviewing. Note how you'd verify the current process.
problems.hint: Use careers pages/blogs/talks; map emphasis to track (trading→math/games, dev/systems→C++/systems/DS&A, research→stats/ML); cite something concrete for 'why'.
problems.tests: Translating firm knowledge into targeted prep.

approach: For each firm, capture: (a) business — market maker (e.g., Optiver/IMC/Citadel Securities), prop/low-latency trader (HRT/Jump), or quant fund (Two Sigma/DE Shaw); (b) target role on your track; (c) likely interview emphasis — trading roles → fast mental math, probability/EV, and market-making/estimation games; quant dev/systems → high-bar DS&A plus C++/systems and possibly a systems-design/'make it fast' round; research → statistics/ML, modeling rigor, avoiding overfitting/lookahead; (d) a specific, authentic reason (a product, paper, talk, tech stack, or team) — not generic praise; (e) module review plan.

Module mapping: trading/research → Quant-Math (probability, Bayes, mental math, market-making games) and Strategies/microstructure; quant dev/systems → C++ section, Systems section, Architecture section, plus the Algorithms module for DS&A and the low-latency coding-patterns and systems-design lessons here; research → Strategies (alpha signals, backtesting) and stats.

Verify the current process: read each firm's careers page and any recruiter communications, check engineering/research blogs and recent public talks, and treat community reports (Glassdoor/forums) as priors to confirm, not facts. Then prepare the durable track skills rather than memorizing a rumored question set, and craft a specific 'why this firm' for each.

complexity.time: A few hours of research + targeted review

problems.title: Compare two firms and decide where to apply
problems.statement: You're a strong C++/systems-leaning candidate who also enjoys some markets reasoning. Compare a low-latency prop-trading/engineering-heavy firm (HRT/Jump-style) with an options market maker known for trading games and mental math (Optiver/IMC-style). For each: the role you'd target, what their process emphasizes, why you might fit, and which module sections you'd prioritize. Then make and justify a decision.
problems.hint: Match your strengths (C++/systems) to the role and process; weight prep accordingly; pick where your edge is strongest while staying authentic.
problems.tests: Translating firm differences into a personal decision.

approach: Low-latency prop/engineering firm (HRT/Jump-style): target a quant developer / core-systems engineer role. Process emphasis: high-bar DS&A, deep C++ (cost/memory model, templates), systems/performance (caches, lock-free, kernel bypass, measurement), and a systems-design / 'make it fast' round. You'd fit because your C++/systems strength is the core bar. Prioritize: Modern C++, Low-Latency Systems, Architecture sections, plus the low-latency coding-patterns and systems-design lessons, and timed DS&A from the Algorithms module.

Options market maker (Optiver/IMC-style): for a *trading* role, the process emphasizes fast mental math (e.g., Optiver's arithmetic test), probability/EV, and live market-making games — less about your C++. They also hire developers, where C++/systems matters. If you target the trading role, your C++ edge is largely irrelevant to the bar and you'd compete on math/games where you're less differentiated; if you target their dev role, it's closer to the first firm. Prioritize (trading): the Quant-Math section (mental math, EV, Bayes, market-making games) and microstructure; (dev): same as the first firm.

Decision and justification: as a C++/systems-leaning candidate, apply primarily to the engineering-heavy prop firm's quant-dev role (and equivalent dev roles at the market maker), because that's where your demonstrable edge meets their bar — you maximize your hit rate by competing on your strength. Keep enough markets/probability literacy to be credible and to enjoy the domain, but don't pivot to a pure trading role where mental-math speed is the filter and your advantage doesn't apply, unless you genuinely want to trade and will drill that bar. The principle: pick the role whose core bar matches your strongest skills, weight prep ~70% to it, stay authentic about why, and apply broadly within that track (including smaller shops).
